titel: W. David Marx: Fashion Is Bigger Than Ever — but Worse at Rewarding Invention

einzeiler: How Japan pioneered modern street and luxury style — and why global culture stopped…
kurzfassung: Cultural historian W. David Marks looks back at two decades in Tokyo, tracing how Japan shaped global menswear, streetwear, and luxury markets. He discusses his new book Blank Space, arguing that contemporary culture prioritizes profit and entertainment over true artistic invention. Finally, he shares insights on how the fashion industry is struggling with the contradictions of massive corporate growth.
stichpunkte: W. David Marks moved to Tokyo from Florida after a high school exchange program and later authored books on Japanese consumer culture.
Japan served as a leading indicator for global trends, pioneering middle-class luxury consumption, menswear, and modern streetwear.
Bathing Ape and Nego revolutionized store design, packaging, and hype culture, later influencing American hip-hop stars like Pharrell Williams and Kanye West.
Marks's new book Blank Space argues that 21st-century culture has replaced artistic excellence and avant-garde invention with entertainment, money-making, and politics.
The book has faced polarized criticism from all political and cultural sides for its provocative stance on artistic standards.
Marks believes the internet and social media have devalued cultural capital, though real-life social capital and physical spaces remain valuable.
Mass-market luxury faces a fundamental contradiction where shareholder-driven growth dilutes the exclusivity and desirability that define luxury goods.
Independent brands and smaller retailers are returning to sustainable, small-scale production models that bypass massive corporate conglomerates.
For foreigners wanting to build a life in Tokyo, learning the language and understanding deep Japanese cultural references remains the ultimate asset.

clips.text: The guest explains that his hometown in Florida was naturally filled with preppy apparel, though nobody regarded it as fashion at the time.
The conversation shifts to the structural evolution of Japanese society, contrasting traditional quiet wealth with modern startup and crypto fortunes.
An anecdote highlights how older jazz musicians immediately recognized early hip-hop records as a groundbreaking avant-garde progression in music.

clips.hook: The fatal flaw of luxury conglomerates
clips.text: The discussion outlines the inherent mathematical struggle of publicly traded luxury firms that must constantly expand unit sales while preserving rarity.

clips.hook: The real secret to living in Tokyo
clips.text: The speaker advises that moving to Japan requires taking the time to properly master reading and writing rather than treating language as a mere tool.

beschreibung:
In the summer of 2007, BoF founder Imran Amed landed in Tokyo for the first time. A young American writer named W. David Marx took him on a menswear tour of the city's back streets of Shibuya and Harajuku. That trip would eventually lead Marx to become BoF's first contributor — apart from Amed himself.

Nearly 20 years on, Marx is still in Tokyo, watching a city that experienced three of fashion's biggest shifts before anywhere else: luxury as a middle-class product, the rise — and now retreat — of streetwear and menswear as a global obsession. Marx is the author of three books on Japanese and global culture. The first, “Ametora,” is about how Japan absorbed, and then improved, American style. The most recent, “Blank Space,” is a cultural history of the 21st century, arguing that something has gone missing from the way we make culture today.

Amed sat down with Marx in Tokyo to discuss all of this and more in what is a fascinating conversation about the state of global culture and global fashion today, and how Japan’s place in it has changed.

Key Insights:
Japan taught the luxury industry that luxury could be a mass-market business. Marx traces Japan's luxury boom back to the 1970s, when newly wealthy Japanese travellers began bringing home souvenirs from Paris. He argues Japan is where brands like Louis Vuitton first learned that "luxury could become a middle class market," building duty-free stores in airports rather than relying solely on flagship boutiques for old-money customers — a model since exported across the world.

Tokyo Was the Origin Point of the Global Streetwear Boom: Marx lays out how Bathing Ape's underground Tokyo stores became a phenomenon so outsized it reshaped how the rest of the world thought about streetwear. He recalls a Stüssy veteran saying, "Bathing Ape blew streetwear out of the water."

Luxury's growth problem is structural, not cyclical. Marx argues luxury goods are fundamentally different from something like an iPhone, because "for every additional handbag you sell to a new consumer, you do decrease the value of the handbag that you sold originally." That tension between scarcity and growth, he says, “is at the root of the industry's current slump”.

Culture Has a ‘Blank Space’ Where Invention Used to Be: Marx’s central argument is that value shifts, not a lack of talent, have pushed culture away from art for art's sake. He points to hip-hop and graffiti as movements built by outsiders pursuing invention for its own sake, contrasting that with today's incentives: "If you are making things to get attention, if you're making things to make money, it's just very unlikely that your strategy's going to be to be the most inventive as it could possibly be."

Three Books W. David Marx Recommends
Fashion is Spinach, by Elizabeth Hawes
On Human Finery, by Quentin Bell
For a Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign, by Jean Baudrillard
